title: IonForge x Redwood: integration evaluation sync
next_steps: Redwood to share draft partner integration runbook and GPU instance sizing spreadsheet
IonForge to provide network topology and private peering constraints
Schedule on-site perf check (if needed) week of Aug 23
action_items: Maya Chen | Send partner integration runbook and rack-level spec | 2027-08-11
Liam O'Connor | Prep quick perf-estimate spreadsheet (quantization & expected tokens) | 2027-08-10
Priya Rao | Share IonForge VPC peering diagram and compliance checklist | 2027-08-09
summary: Introductory technical discovery between Redwood and IonForge to scope an integration for Redwood runtime on IonForge managed GPU pools. Main topics: connectivity model (VPC peering vs private link), supported GPU SKUs, quantization and kernel compatibility, batching/latency tradeoffs, SSO/KMS requirements, and a proposed pilot timeline.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, with Liam and Zoe. How's the audio?
[00:05] Priya Rao: Good, thanks. Marco and Dana here as well. We got Owen on video but he might be muted.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Awesome. Quick agenda: intro, IonForge constraints, runtime compatibility questions, security/compliance, and next steps. We'll try to keep to 45, run over if needed. Sound okay?
[00:20] Marco Silva: Yeah that's fine. We're mainly interested in how Redwood could run on our managed GPU pools and what work we need to do on the network side.
[00:28] Liam O'Connor: Cool. Very high level — Redwood's serving runtime supports hosted, dedicated, and private. For partner integrations like yours we often run a Private control plane with customer-managed compute or we run a co-located runtime on partner infra. Key pieces: GPU drivers, NCCL for multi-GPU, and kernel compatibility for quantized models.
[00:45] Dana Kim: When you say kernel compatibility, are you referring to specific CUDA/cuDNN versions or more like operator-level differences?
[00:52] Liam O'Connor: A bit of both — some quantized kernels need recent CUDA + specific JIT kernels. We also switch kernels based on model architecture; for example transformer attention kernels differ for 8-bit quant paths. Occasionally there's a mismatch with older drivers which causes subtle perf or numerics.
[01:07] Priya Rao: Our fleet runs a mix of A100s and RTX 6000 equivalents — some older cards still on 470.x drivers because of legacy infra. That might be an issue?
[01:15] Zoe Park: It can be. For the quantized 4-bit path we recommend driver 525+ and matching cuBLAS/cuDNN; otherwise we fall back to FP16 kernels which increase memory and cost. We can provide a compatibility matrix.
[01:28] Marco Silva: Great. On networking — we prefer not to open public endpoints. Our typical pattern is private peering + internal DNS. Is that supported?
[01:36] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We've done both private peering/VPC peering and private link-style setups for partners. For IonForge we can support a private control plane option where the control plane sits in Redwood-managed account but only accepts connections from your IP ranges, or we can run an all-on-prem agent.
[01:51] Owen Li (Speaker 1): Quick interjection — for multi-tenant concerns, how do you isolate KV caches and model weights from other tenants?
[01:57] Liam O'Connor: Good question. We use namespace isolation for KV caches and encrypted model artifacts per tenant. For partner-hosted deployments we can use customer-managed KMS so keys never leave your boundary. There's also optional cgroups and GPU partitioning depending on the vendor.
[02:12] Dana Kim: You mentioned model artifacts — does Redwood push model binaries to the partner infra or do we pull them from S3?
[02:18] Zoe Park: We do either. For compliance-heavy customers we prefer the customer-supplied S3 or minio pull; we orchestrate a pull with signed URLs and attestations. For partners with secure supply chains we can also ship pre-staged images but that requires signing and agreed provenance.
[02:33] Marco Silva: Okay. On the performance side: we have customers that need low single-digit latency tail at 2–4 tokens per request and also bats of smaller requests. How does Redwood handle batching vs latency?
[02:44] Liam O'Connor: The runtime uses continuous batching with configurable latency SLOs. You can set a per-route latency target, and the runtime will trade some throughput. Also we do prefix KV caching to reduce repeated compute for similar prompts. For heavy tail-sensitive workloads we suggest dedicated capacity.
[02:58] Priya Rao: Dedicated is, like, reserved GPUs? Do you provide autoscaling?
[03:03] Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated means reserved GPU pools for your tenant with optional autoscaling and burst. For partner integrations we sometimes do shared pools with strict RBAC and quotas — it's a cost tradeoff.
[03:12] Marco Silva: What about billing and metering in a partner setup? We would need token-level usage data for chargeback.
[03:18] Zoe Park: We expose token-level metering and per-route cost breakdowns through the Console. If running on your infra we can plug into your billing endpoint or export logs to your SIEM.
[03:28] Owen Li (Speaker 1): Are there any telemetry or agents we need to install to get those metrics?
[03:32] Liam O'Connor: There's a lightweight agent for metrics and traces; it's optional. We also support exporting Prometheus metrics or pushing to logs to your S3.
[03:39] Marco Silva: Security — SOC2, SSO, KMS — what's required from our side?
[03:44] Maya Chen: We are SOC2 certified; for partners we commonly integrate via SAML SSO and customer-managed KMS. We have an audit log export and can provide a SOC2 report and pen test summary. I'll drop the security pack after the call.
[03:56] Priya Rao: That'd be great. Also any redaction or retention policies? We need to ensure PII isn't stored beyond X days in our environment.
[04:03] Zoe Park: Retention is configurable. For private deployments you control storage; for hosted we offer retention windows and on-write redaction hooks. We'll share the retention config doc.
[04:12] Marco Silva: Back to integration specifics — how do you handle model versioning and rollouts inside partner environments?
[04:19] Liam O'Connor: We support pinned model versions, canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback to a compatible variant. For partner-hosted environments we recommend a staging cluster where rollouts are validated with a smoke test harness.
[04:32] Dana Kim: We have strong gating around model weights and provenance. Any support for signature verification of weights?
[04:38] Zoe Park: Yes, we can verify model signatures and attest manifests. We also support immutable model bundles and content-addressed storage to ensure integrity.
[04:47] Marco Silva: Competitor question — some partners use Run:AI or NVIDIA fleet manager. How do you differentiate?
[04:53] Maya Chen: We're focused on inference runtime and dev ergonomics for LLMs — the kernel pathing, KV cache, and batching strategies are tuned for production LLM traffic. Tools like Run:AI focus on job scheduling and GPU virtualization; we can interop with them at the scheduler level.
[05:08] Priya Rao: Any constraints on orchestration layer? We run Nomad and some k8s clusters.
[05:13] Liam O'Connor: We support k8s and have a Nomad adapter used in one partner; we can provide a helm chart and operator or a standalone runtime container.
[05:21] Owen Li (Speaker 1): We also need to know which quantization formats you support — 4-bit LLM.int8?
[05:27] Liam O'Connor: We have an internal quantization pipeline that supports 4-bit and mixed int8/4-bit modes; some older ops end up in fallback. We'll provide a model/quantization recommendation based on the model family.
[05:38] Marco Silva: Nice. For the pilot, what's the minimum scope you'd propose?
[05:43] Maya Chen: Typical pilot: 2 models (a 2B and a 13B), one end-to-end route, and a synthetic workload to validate 95th percentile latency and cost. Duration 3–4 weeks. We provide bench scripts and sample prompts.
[05:58] Dana Kim: Would you need physical access to our rack or can it be done purely remotely?
[06:02] Zoe Park: Usually remote is sufficient, we ask for remote SSH and access to the cluster, but we can do an on-site visit if there's network security blocking remote connections.
[06:11] Marco Silva: Ok good. Any regulatory concerns for EU customers specifically? Data residency etc.
[06:16] Maya Chen: We have region-aware deployments and can commit to data residency in EU regions; for partner infra we can run within your EU datacenter. We'll align to your compliance questionnaire.
[06:25] Priya Rao: One niggle — our customers use tokenization variations; how much control do we retain over preprocessors?
[06:31] Liam O'Connor: You own the preprocessors — we integrate via a plugin or pre-tokenization step. We can also host the tokenizer as a sidecar for deterministic behavior.
[06:41] Marco Silva: Performance numbers — can you ballpark token/s for a single A100 with your optimized kernels on a 13B?
[06:48] Liam O'Connor: Rough; with FP16 and attention optimizations you might see 30–50 tok/s depending on prompt length. With 4-bit quant and tuned kernels that can go up to ~70 tok/s. We'll provide a more accurate spreadsheet tied to your sequence length distribution.
[07:03] Owen Li (Speaker 1): Sequence length distribution — we typically see many short requests (~50 tokens) plus some long ones. Do you support per-route sequence caps?
[07:10] Zoe Park: Yes, route-level caps and dynamic truncation policies exist.
[07:13] Speaker 2: Sorry, just fyi we'll want to test memory fragmentation on long running daemons.
[07:18] Liam O'Connor: Noted. We monitor memory fragmentation and have recommendations for garbage collection intervals and process restarts for long-lived runtimes.
[07:26] Maya Chen: Quick pause — I see a chat link question about pricing. For partners pricing can be reciprocal. We typically share a partner rate card for pilot and then discuss revenue share if you're reselling. I'll include a draft.
[07:40] Marco Silva: Revenue share would be interesting, but first we need to validate technical fit.
[07:44] Priya Rao: Agreed. Also curious about support SLAs for partner-hosted tenants.
[07:50] Zoe Park: We offer 24/7 support for Dedicated with a defined P1/P2 SLA. For partner integrations we can negotiate an SLA based on committed capacity.
[07:59] Dana Kim: Any hard limits on batch size or token windows in the runtime?
[08:03] Liam O'Connor: Batch size is configurable but constrained by GPU memory. We provide heuristics and an auto-tuner to select batch sizes for best throughput within latency SLOs.
[08:14] Marco Silva: Good. On the ops side — how are rollbacks handled if a new model causes errors?
[08:18] Liam O'Connor: We keep immutable model bundles and use traffic shifting plus instant rollback. There's also automated health checks that can auto-fallback to previous versions.
[08:26] Owen Li (Speaker 1): Are there any special kernel licenses or binary blobs we need to distribute to partners?
[08:32] Liam O'Connor: We rely on standard vendor drivers; we don't ship proprietary kernel blobs beyond typical CUDA/cuDNN. For some low-level fused kernels we use prebuilt kernels which we can distribute under partner NDA if needed.
[08:45] Priya Rao: That might need procurement review. We'll flag it.
[08:48] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll include license specifics in the runbook.
[08:52] Marco Silva: Great. Any direct customer references or partner case studies you can share for a similar integration?
[08:58] Zoe Park: Yes — we recently integrated with a telco partner running a private edge GPU pool; I'll include a short case study PDF and a contact.
[09:07] Priya Rao: Awesome. For the pilot timeline — if we start mid-August what are realistic milestones?
[09:13] Maya Chen: Week 1: infra prep and access; Week 2: model staging and smoke tests; Week 3: load/perf tests; Week 4: review and tuning. So start Aug 16 yields completion mid-September.
[09:26] Marco Silva: Sounds reasonable. One last technical — do you support mixed precision fallback for ops that don't have quantized kernels?
[09:33] Liam O'Connor: Yes, dynamic fallback to FP16/FP32 for unsupported ops; we track fallback rates in the Console so you can see regression impact.
[09:42] Owen Li (Speaker 1): Perfect. We'll want visibility into fallback rates during the pilot.
[09:46] Zoe Park: We'll enable telemetry and a quick dashboard.
[09:50] Maya Chen: Cool. Closing loop — to summarise: Redwood sends runbook, compat matrix, and pricing draft; IonForge shares VPC diagram and driver inventory; schedule pilot kickoff week of Aug 16. Any other asks?
[10:03] Marco Silva: Please also send the kernel/driver version matrix.
[10:06] Priya Rao: And SOC2 report.
[10:08] Dana Kim: We'll review and get procurement looped in.
[10:12] Maya Chen: Perfect. I'll capture action items and follow up with links. Thanks everyone.
[10:16] Speaker 3: Thanks. Bye.

Notes: transcript has minor speaker labeling errors and artifacts from auto-transcription. Links mentioned in chat: https://redwood.ai/partners/runbook (placeholder), https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 (placeholder).
